rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses leaves Pharaoh’s reminder of his upbringing unanswered because a messenger’s proof is unaffected by whether the addressee once benefited him.
rows.anchor: فصار قول فرعون لما قاله غير مؤثر ألبتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s ‘I did it then while among the astray’ means he was unaware that the disciplinary blow would lead to death.
rows.anchor: والمراد بذلك الذاهلين عن معرفة ما يؤول إليه من القتل لأنه فعل الوكزة على وجه التأديب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Moses struck for discipline, he says the act should not make him liable, a disbeliever, or ungrateful for Pharaoh’s favor.
rows.anchor: فبين له أنه فعله على وجه لا يجوز معه أن يؤاخذ به أو يعد منه كافرا أو كافرا لنعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says his flight followed Pharaoh’s threat after the chiefs plotted to kill him; the threat itself caused his fear and flight.
rows.anchor: ومع ذلك فررت منكم عند قولكم : { إن الملا يأتمرون بك ليقتلوك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thus Pharaoh had no favor concerning the killing: his conduct was closer to wrongdoing because he frightened Moses into fleeing.
rows.anchor: فبين بذلك أنه لا نعمة له عليه في باب تلك الفعلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Moses fled, God benefited him by granting judgment and making him a messenger, while Pharaoh had wronged him.
rows.anchor: ثم بين نعمة الله تعالى عليه بعد الفرار ، فكأنه قال أسأتم وأحسن الله إلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers that ‘judgment’ means knowledge rather than prophethood, since prophethood is separately stated in the next clause.
rows.anchor: والأقرب أنه غير النبوة لأن المعطوف غير المعطوف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The knowledge intended includes reason, judgment, and religious knowledge of divine unity; God would not send Moses without these perfections.
rows.anchor: فالمراد بالحكم العلم ويدخل في العلم العقل والرأي والعلم بالدين الذي هو التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ‘bestowed’ expressly indicates that God created this judgment in Moses.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { فوهب لى ربى حكما } كالتنصيص على أن ذلك الحكم من خلق الله تعالى

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites interpret the judgment as divine graces (luṭf); Razi calls this very weak because grace is given to all without withholding, so its specification needs a reason.
rows.anchor: وقالت المعتزلة : المراد منه الألطاف وهو ضعيف جدا لأن الألطاف مفعولة في حق الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s reply answers Pharaoh’s claim that he raised him: Pharaoh took him into his care because he had enslaved Israel and killed their sons.
rows.anchor: أحدها : أنه إنما وقع في يده وفي تربيته لأنه قصد تعبيد بني إسرائيل وذبح أبنائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that Pharaoh’s later kindness is outweighed and cancelled by his earlier great oppression of Israel’s ancestors.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : أن هذا الإنعام المتأخر صار معاضا بذلك الظلم العظيم على أسلافنا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Pharaoh enslaved the Israelites, took their wealth, and spent some of it on Moses, so the upbringing was no favor.
rows.anchor: ما قاله الحسن : إنك استعبدتهم وأخذت أموالهم ومنها أنفقت علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Moses was actually raised by his mother and fellow Israelites whom Pharaoh enslaved; Pharaoh merely refrained from killing him.
rows.anchor: المراد أن الذي تولى تربيتي هم الذين قد استعبدتهم فلا نعمة لك علي لأن التربية كانت من قبل أمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final explanation: Pharaoh claimed Israel as his slaves, and a master earns no gratitude merely by feeding and supplying a slave.
rows.anchor: أنك كنت تدعي أن بني إسرائيل عبيدك ولا منة للمولى على العبد في أن يطعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows that an unbeliever’s disbelief does not erase the favor he did; Moses rejects Pharaoh’s claim by other arguments.
rows.anchor: في الآية دلالة على أن كفر الكافر لا يبطل نعمته على من يحسن إليه ولا يبطل منته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars say an unbeliever deserves humiliation, not thanks for kindness, since thanks entails reverence and would conflict with the humiliation due for disbelief.
rows.anchor: إذا كان كافرا لا يستحق الشكر على نعمه على الناس إنما يستحق الإهانة بكفره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other scholars hold that disbelief does not cancel gratitude for kindness, only the reward and praise earned through faith; Razi says the verse supports this view.
rows.anchor: لا يبطل الشكر بالكفر وإنما يبطل بالكفر الثواب والمدح الذي يستحقه على الإيمان

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf explains the plural ‘from you’ and ‘I feared you’ as including Pharaoh and the chiefs who plotted, while the singular favor and enslavement refer to Pharaoh alone.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) إنما جمع الضمير في { منكم } و { خفتكم } مع إفراده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘That’ points to an unspecified disgraceful act, and ‘that you enslaved’ is its appositional clarification; the phrase means enslaving Israel is the favor Pharaoh claims.
rows.anchor: ( تلك ) إشارة إلى خصلة شنعاء مبهمة لا يدرى ما هي إلا بتفسيرها وهي { أن عبدت } فإن { أن عبدت } عطف بيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi cites the appositional construction in God’s decree to Lot as a parallel grammatical example.
rows.anchor: ونظيره قوله تعالى : { وقضينآ إليه ذلك الامر أن دابر هؤلآء مقطوع مصبحين }

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj offers another syntax: ‘that’ may be accusative, meaning Pharaoh’s action became a favor only because he enslaved Israel; without it Moses’s family would have sufficed.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج : ويحوز أن يكون ( أن ) في موضع نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh asks what the Lord of the worlds is only after Moses has already summoned him to worship that Lord.
rows.anchor: فأتيا فرعون فقولا إنا رسول رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi considers that Pharaoh knew God but asked for political power; on the reading with fatḥah in ‘you knew’ Pharaoh knows, while the nominative reading makes Moses the knower who informed him.
rows.anchor: فإذا قرىء بفتح التاء من { علمت } فالمراد أن فرعون علم ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi argues that a rational Pharaoh necessarily knew he had not always existed and had acquired life and reason, so he had to infer a cause for his constitution and faculties.
rows.anchor: فلا بد وأن يتولد له من هذين العلمين علم ثالث بافتقاره في تركيبه وفي حياته وعقله إلى مؤثر موجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible account is that Pharaoh followed the Dahriyya, treating celestial spheres as self-existent and their own motions as causes of worldly events.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يقال إنه كان على مذهب الدهرية من أن الأفلاك واجبة الوجود في ذواتها ومتحركة لذواتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility is a philosopher’s doctrine of a necessary, non-volitional cause; Pharaoh then claimed local divinity through enslaving and ruling his people.
rows.anchor: أو يقال إنه كان من الفلاسفة القائلين بالعلة الموجبة لا بالفاعل المختار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi also proposes that Pharaoh held an incarnation doctrine: God inhabits a particular human body as a soul inhabits a body, and so Pharaoh called himself divine.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يقال إنه كان على مذهب الحلولية ، القائلين بأن ذات الإله يتدرع بجسد إنسان معين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question ‘what is it?’ seeks a thing’s essence, which could be defined by itself, its parts, something external, or a combination of internal and external features.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن السؤال بما طلب لتعريف حقيقة الشيء ، وتعريف حقيقة الشيء إما أن يكون بنفس تلك الحقيقة أو بشيء من أجزائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defining the Necessary Existent through internal parts is impossible: a composite depends on components and is therefore possible, whereas the Necessary is not composite.
rows.anchor: لأن كل مركب فهو محتاج إلى كل واحد من أجزائه ، وكل واحد من أجزائه فهو غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God cannot be defined by himself or parts, he can be identified only through clear external concomitants; the most evident effect is the sensible cosmos, making Moses’s answer the only possible one.
rows.anchor: لا يمكن تعريف ماهية واجب الوجود إلا بلوازمه وآثاره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘If you are certain’ means that accepting these sensible things as ending in the Necessary entails that the Necessary is absolutely one and can only be made known by its clearest effects.
rows.anchor: لما سلمتم انتهاء هذه المحسوسات إلى الواجب لذاته ، ثبت أن الواجب لذاته فرد مطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s ‘Do you not listen?’ expresses amazement: he asked for essence and Moses answered with causal agency.
rows.anchor: يعني أنا أطلب منه الماهية وخصوصية الحقيقة ، وهو يجيبني بالفاعلية والمؤثرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi raises the objection that describing God by effects does not disclose the essence: knowing something has an effect either only identifies it circularly or fails to identify its particular nature.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن التعريف بالوصف الخارجي لا يفيد معرفة نفس الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses shifts to God as the creator of people and ancestors because someone might regard the heavens as self-existent, but cannot regard himself and his forebears as beginningless; what begins and ends needs a cause.
rows.anchor: لا يمكن أن يعتقد العاقل في نفسه وأبيه وأجداده كونهم واجبين لذواتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh calls Moses mad because he says Moses fails to answer the request for God’s specific essence with those external effects.
rows.anchor: فهذا الذي يدعي الرسالة مجنون لا يفهم السؤال فضلا عن أن يجيب عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s third proof points to the sun’s regular rising and setting, whose remarkable ongoing order requires a governor; Razi compares it to Abraham’s argument against Nimrod.
rows.anchor: الأمر ظاهر في أن هذا التدبير المستمر على الوجه العجيب لا يتم إلا بتدبير مدبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi links Moses’s proof from human creation and death to Abraham’s first proof, and Moses’s proof from sunrise and sunset to Abraham’s decisive second proof.
rows.anchor: فإن الله يأتي بالشمس من المشرق فأت بها من المغرب فبهت الذي كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘If you reason’ means that a rational listener must accept the effects-based answer, since neither God’s essence nor its parts can define it.
rows.anchor: فكأنه عليه السلام قال إن كنت من العقلاء عرفت أنه لا جواب عن سؤالك إلا ما ذكرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says the divine essence as it is in itself is beyond human comprehension, as he also explains under ‘the All-Subduing above His servants.’
rows.anchor: حقيقة الإله سبحانه من حيث هي هي غير معقولة للبشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger’s claim needs proof that the worlds have a Lord, not knowledge of that Lord’s particular essence; Moses supplies what validates his mission while Pharaoh asks an irrelevant question.
rows.anchor: ادعاء رسالة رب العالمين تتوقف صحته على إثبات أن للعالمين ربا وإلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Moses’s pointed challenge, Pharaoh abandons argument and threatens imprisonment because he has failed in debate.
rows.anchor: فإنه لما عجز عن الحجاج عدل إلى التخويف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s ‘even if I bring a clear thing’ asks whether Pharaoh would imprison him despite his ability to present clear proof of God and his messengership.
rows.anchor: هل تستجيز أن تسجنني مع اقتداري على أن آتيك بأمر بين في باب الدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh accepts the challenge by demanding the proof if Moses is truthful.
rows.anchor: فأت به إن كنت من الصادقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exchange implies God is not a body: if God had a form, Moses could have stated his essence and Pharaoh’s complaint would be valid.
rows.anchor: الآية تدل على أنه تعالى ليس بجسم لأنه لو كان جسما وله صورة لكان جواب موسى عليه السلام بذكر حقيقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A caller to God should not answer foolish abuse: Moses continues giving proofs when called mad and when threatened with prison.
rows.anchor: الواجب على من يدعو غيره إلى الله تعالى أن لا يجيب عن السفاهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A respondent may change from one example to another to clarify an argument; doing so does not show defeat.
rows.anchor: يجوز للمسؤول أن يعدل في حجته من مثال إلى مثال لإيضاح الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a miracle seems unrelated to the earlier proofs, the staff’s transformation would prove God, divine unity, and Moses’s truthfulness; this conclusion is stronger and more comprehensive.
rows.anchor: انقلاب العصا حية على الله تعالى وعلى توحيده ، وعلى أنه صادق في الرسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What is between them’ uses the dual because it means the space between the two directions.
rows.anchor: أريد ما بين الجهتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses first generalizes to all creation, then specifies people and ancestors as closest and most observable, and then sunrise and sunset as especially clear signs through their ordered seasonal course.
rows.anchor: قد عمم أولا ثم خصص من العام للبيان أنفسهم وآباءهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘I will make you one of the imprisoned’ evokes Pharaoh’s notorious practice of putting prisoners alone in a deep, dark well, a fate worse than death.
rows.anchor: وكان من عادته أن يأخذ من يريد أن يسجنه فيطرحه في بئر عميقة فردا لا يبصر فيها ولا يسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waw in ‘or even if I brought you’ is circumstantial after the interrogative hamza: ‘Would you do this to me while I come with a clear thing?’
rows.anchor: السابع : الواو في قوله : { أو * لو * جئتك } واو الحال دخلت عليها همزة الاستفهام

none: Qur’anic verse text only; no commentary point is stated in this segment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story of Moses follows Muhammad’s grief over his people’s unbelief to show him that Moses endured the same trial; Abraham’s story follows to show an even greater grief.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه ذكر قصة موسى عليه السلام ليعرف محمد أن مثل تلك المحنة كانت حاصلة لموسى : ثم ذكر عقبها قصة إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham faced the pain of seeing his father and people headed for the Fire while only able to call and warn them.
rows.anchor: أن يرى أباه وقومه في النار وهو لا يتمكن من إنقاذهم إلا بقدر الدعاء والتنبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham already knew they worshipped idols; he asked what they worshipped to expose that their objects did not deserve worship, as a question can set up a revealing analogy.
rows.anchor: وكان إبراهيم عليه السلام يعلم أنهم عبدة أصنام ولكنه سألهم ليريهم أن ما يعبدونه ليس من استحقاق العبادة في شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi compares Abraham’s question to asking a slave trader what he owns, knowing the answer is slaves, then showing that slaves are merchandise rather than property.
rows.anchor: كما تقول لتاجر الرقيق ما مالك ؟ وأنت تعلم أن ماله الرقيق ، ثم تقول : الرقيق جمال وليس بمال .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘To remain devoted’ means to stay at something; they said ‘we remain’ because they worshipped idols in daytime, not at night.
rows.anchor: والعكوف : الإقامة على الشيء ، وإنما قالوا : { * نظل } لأنهم كانوا يعبدونها بالنهار دون الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their unnecessary addition that they remained devoted displayed their inward delight and pride in idol worship.
rows.anchor: ضموا إليه زيادة على الجواب وهي قولهم : { أصناما فنظل لها عاكفين } وإنما ذكروا هذه الزيادة إظهارا لما في نفوسهم من الابتهاج والافتخار

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf says ‘Do they hear you?’ requires an omitted noun: ‘Do they hear your supplication when you call?’
rows.anchor: لا بد في يسمعونكم من تقدير حذف المضاف معناه هل يسمعون دعاءكم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah reads the question as asking whether the idols hear and answer their supplication.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة { هل يسمعونكم } أي هل يسمعونكم الجواب عن دعائكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reasoning is that worshippers seek help from those they worship, expecting them to hear their requests and grant benefit or avert harm; idols cannot fulfill this role.
rows.anchor: يلتجىء إليه في المسألة ليعرف مراده إذا سمع دعاءه ثم يستجيب له في بذل منفعة أو دفع مضرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people answer the proof by appealing to their ancestors; this demonstrates the error of blind imitation and the duty to use evidence.
rows.anchor: وهذا من أقوى الدلائل على فساد التقليد ووجوب التمسك بالاستدلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If imitation were praised and reasoning condemned, one would praise the unbelievers’ condemned way and condemn Abraham’s praised way.
rows.anchor: لكان ذلك مدحا لطريقة الكفار التي ذمها الله تعالى وذما لطريقة إبراهيم عليه السلام التي مدحها الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s reply teaches that falsehood does not become true by being old or new, or by having many or few adherents.
rows.anchor: أن الباطل لا يتغير بأن يكون قديما أو حديثا ، ولا بأن يكون في فاعلية كثرة أو قلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One answer to how an inanimate idol can be an enemy is that God will resurrect idols to disavow and rebuke their worshippers in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: إن الله يحيي ما عبدوه من الأصنام حتى يقع منهم التوبيخ لهم والبراءة منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another answer: idolaters treat idols as living beings by glorifying and hoping in them; since idols lead them from happiness to misery, they function as enemies.
rows.anchor: لما نزلت هذه الأصنام منزلة الأحياء وجرت مجرى الدافع للمنفعة والجالب للمضرة لا جرم جرت مجرى الأعداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation takes ‘they’ to mean the idol worshippers themselves; the wording follows the immediately preceding mention of the things worshipped.
rows.anchor: المراد في قوله : { فإنهم عدو لى } عداوة من يعبدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham says the idols are enemies to himself, not his audience, to portray this as advice he first gave himself and thereby make it more persuasive to them.
rows.anchor: إني فكرت في أمري فرأيت عبادتي لها عبادة للعدو فاجتنبتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Enemy’ is grammatically singular though it refers to many; Razi cites poetry and ‘they are an enemy to you’ as parallels, referring back to his discussion of ‘we are the messenger.’
rows.anchor: العدو والصديق يجيئان في معنى الواحد والجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi cites a poetic line using singular ‘enemy’ of a group to support the singular-for-plural usage.
rows.anchor: أراهم عدوا وكانوا صديقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is disconnected and means ‘but the Lord of the worlds.’
rows.anchor: استثناء منقطع كأنه قال لكن رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning the Lord of the worlds, Abraham describes God by qualities that make him worthy of worship; the passage announces four qualities and begins with creation and guidance.
rows.anchor: ما وصفه به مما يستحق العبادة لأجله ، ثم حكى عنه ما سأله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation and guidance together provide all benefits to every being capable of receiving benefit.
rows.anchor: الخلق والهداية بهما يحصل جميع المنافع لكل من يصح الانتفاع عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the human belongs to the bodily realm of creation; others say the spiritual realm of command. The body’s formation precedes the heart’s reception of spirit.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من قال هو من عالم الخلق والجسمانيات ، ومن قال هو من عالم الأمر الروحانيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi reads ‘when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit’ as bodily composition followed by the divine luminous subtlety from the realm of command.
rows.anchor: فالتسوية إشارة إلى تعديل المزاج وتركيب الأمشاج ، ونفخ الروح إشارة إلى اللطيفة الربانية النورانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses about the human’s clay origin and later bodily stages point to the spirit from the angelic realm; guidance comes through the spirit, showing creation precedes guidance.
rows.anchor: وذلك إشارة إلى الروح الذي هو من عالم الملائكة ، ولا شك أن الهداية إنما تحصل من الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi links God’s praise as creator and guide here to the same pairing in the opening verses of al-Aʿlā.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه سبحانه أثنى على نفسه بهذين الأمرين في قوله : { الذى خلق فسوى * والذى قدر فهدى }
